passage:
The exam was over, and the 5:40 bus was full of Hafsa’s laughter. She, Reena and their friend Meher were replaying the maths paper in loud voices, and every joke got louder than the last. Hafsa leaned across the aisle to slap Reena’s shoulder and nearly knocked a woman’s shopping bag.
A woman holding a sleeping toddler glanced up. Then an older man said, gently and with a small smile, “Beta, could you lower it a little? The baby just fell asleep.”
Hafsa went pink. “Oh! Sorry, uncle.” Reena mouthed sorry to the woman, and Meher giggled behind her hand. The rest of the ride was quiet chatter and a few silent grins.

qa.q: What were the girls laughing about on the bus?
qa.a: Hafsa, Reena and Meher were replaying the maths paper after the exam.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa go pink when the older man spoke?
qa.a: Hafsa realised she had been so caught up in the group's fun that she had forgotten the other passengers. She felt embarrassed, and it was thoughtlessness, not meanness.

qa.q: What made the older man's request work well?
qa.a: He spoke gently, smiled, and gave a clear reason, the sleeping baby. That let the girls fix it easily instead of feeling attacked.

qa.q: How might the woman with the toddler have felt before the man spoke?
qa.a: She was probably tired and worried the noise would wake the baby, but she did not want to make a fuss. Her glance upward was the only sign she showed.

grounding: Shows a group of teens laughing loudly on a bus out of thoughtlessness, corrected by one calm word.

“Bro, did you see his face when the truck flipped?” Siddharth said, laughing loud enough to echo.
“Shh, it’s the quiet part,” Hrithik whispered, but he was grinning too.
“Nobody cares! Danish, tell him!” Danish only shrugged and slid lower in his seat.
A woman two rows ahead turned around. “Excuse me, I’m sorry, could you keep it down a little? I can’t hear the dialogue.”
Siddharth blinked. “Oh. Yeah, sure. Sorry, ma’am.”
The row was quiet for a minute. Then Hrithik leaned in, whispering, “Told you.” Siddharth whispered back, “Fine, fine,” and Danish finally smiled.

qa.q: What did the woman ask the boys to do?
qa.a: She asked them to keep it down a little because she could not hear the dialogue.

qa.q: Why did Danish slide lower in his seat when Siddharth turned to him?
qa.a: Danish may have felt uncomfortable being pulled into the loud fun, because he did not join in and just shrugged. The passage does not say for sure why.

qa.q: What made Siddharth change his behaviour so quickly?
qa.a: The woman spoke politely and gave a reason, and it reminded Siddharth that others were watching too. That was easier to accept than a scolding.

qa.q: How did Hrithik see the situation differently from Siddharth?
qa.a: Hrithik noticed the quiet moment and whispered a warning, even while grinning, so he was more aware of the people around them than Siddharth was.

grounding: Shows teenagers laughing loudly in a cinema, enjoying their group energy, and correcting themselves after a calm request.

passage: At the touring tent cinema at the Sirsi fair, Bhavna, Leela and four friends sat in the second row, sharing roasted peanuts and commenting on every scene. When the hero fell off his horse, Leela shrieked with laughter, and the others joined in, stamping their feet on the wooden benches. It was the best night of their summer. Behind them, an old farmer leaned forward and said calmly, 'Girls, I've come twenty kilometres for this film. Let me hear the songs, at least.' Bhavna turned red. She hadn't even thought about the people behind. 'Sorry, ajja,' she said. They whispered through the rest, and at the interval Leela offered the farmer some peanuts.

qa.q: How far had the old farmer come for the film?
qa.a: Twenty kilometres.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna turn red?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and a little guilty, realising she hadn't even thought about the people behind them.

qa.q: Why did the farmer's words work so well?
qa.a: He spoke calmly and gave a real reason, so the girls could apologise instead of getting defensive.

qa.q: What might the evening have been like for the farmer before he spoke?
qa.a: Frustrating, having travelled twenty kilometres and being unable to hear the film over the laughter.

grounding: A group of teenage girls, caught up in their fun, is loud at a fair cinema until a calm word from a farmer corrects it.

passage: On the evening train in Mexico City, Diego, Camila and three classmates were replaying the school football final, loudly, with sound effects. Diego acted out his own goal and bumped into a pole. Camila laughed so hard she snorted, which made everyone laugh more. The carriage was packed with people coming home from work. A nurse in blue scrubs, sitting across from them, closed her eyes and rubbed her temples. At the next stop she said quietly, 'Chicos, twelve-hour shift. Could you bring it down a little?' Diego's grin faded. 'Sorry, señora.' They talked in low voices for the rest of the ride. When the nurse got off, Camila said, 'I didn't even see her.'

qa.q: How long was the nurse's shift?
qa.a: Twelve hours.

qa.q: What did Diego feel when the nurse spoke?
qa.a: His grin faded; he felt embarrassed and sorry, realising how loud they had been.

qa.q: What made the nurse's request effective?
qa.a: She asked quietly, gave a reason and didn't scold, so the group lowered their voices willingly.

qa.q: What was the ride like for the nurse before she spoke?
qa.a: Exhausting, with a headache after a long shift and a loud group right across from her.

grounding: Teenagers celebrating loudly on a train forget others around them until a calm request corrects it.

passage: The four of them had come to the city library to study for the chemistry test, but Dilnaz found an old photo of their teacher in a yearbook, and that was the end of studying. Afreen laughed so hard she snorted, which made Rukhsar laugh harder. Their table shook. Around them, heads lifted: an old man with a newspaper, a college student in earphones, a woman with a toddler asleep on her shoulder. Afreen didn't notice; the joke felt like the best thing all week. Then the librarian, Mr Pinto, walked over and crouched by their table. "Girls, I can see it's funny," he said quietly. "The baby over there just fell asleep. Maybe take the yearbook outside for five minutes?" Afreen looked across. The mother gave a small, tired smile. Afreen's face went warm. "Sorry, sir," she whispered, and they tiptoed out, still shaking with giggles.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz find in the yearbook?
qa.a: An old photo of their teacher.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling before and after Mr Pinto spoke?
qa.a: At first she felt giddy and delighted, then embarrassed once she saw the tired mother.

qa.q: Why did Mr Pinto's approach work?
qa.a: He spoke quietly, admitted the joke was funny, and gave a reason and a simple option, so the girls felt corrected, not shamed.

qa.q: What was it like for the mother with the sleeping toddler?
qa.a: She was probably tired and worried the noise would wake her child, and relieved when the girls stepped outside.

grounding: Shows teenagers laughing loudly in a library, caught up in their group's energy, and a calm word from the librarian correcting it.
